title: Dynamic Programming
scopeHtml: Scope: DP method, 1D and 2D DP, knapsack, longest increasing subsequence.

notes.title: What dynamic programming is
notes.html:
Idea. Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by combining answers to overlapping subproblems and remembering each answer so it is computed once. It applies when the problem has optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best answers to smaller pieces) and the same subproblems repeat.

The five-step method.

  1. State: what do the parameters of a subproblem mean? (dp[i] = best answer for the first i items.)
  2. Transition: how does a state depend on smaller states?
  3. Base cases: the smallest states with known answers.
  4. Order: compute smaller states first (or use recursion with memoization).
  5. Answer: which state holds the final result?

Two styles. Top-down (memoization): write the recursion, cache results. Easy to derive, uses stack depth. Bottom-up (tabulation): fill a table iteratively. Faster in practice and lets you reduce memory by keeping only the last row or last few values.

Worked example: Climbing Stairs (ways to climb n steps taking 1 or 2 at a time). dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]; the naive recursion is exponential, the DP is linear and needs only two variables.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int climbStairs(int n) {
    if (n <= 2) return n;
    int a = 1, b = 2;                                // ways for steps 1 and 2
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}
int climbStairs(int n) {
    if (n <= 2) return n;
    int a = 1, b = 2;                                // ways for steps 1 and 2
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}
fun climbStairs(n: Int): Int {
    if (n <= 2) return n
    var a = 1
    var b = 2                                        // ways for steps 1 and 2
    for (i in 3..n) { val c = a + b; a = b; b = c }
    return b
}
from functools import lru_cache

def climb_stairs(n):
    if n <= 2:
        return n
    a, b = 1, 2                                      # ways for steps 1 and 2
    for _ in range(3, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

@lru_cache(None)                                     # top-down version with memoization
def climb_memo(n):
    return n if n <= 2 else climb_memo(n - 1) + climb_memo(n - 2)

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(2^n) for naive recursion.

Industry examples. Diff tools (longest common subsequence), spell-checkers (edit distance), route and resource optimisation, speech recognition (Viterbi), and text justification in layout engines.

Everyday analogy. Writing down the answer to each sub-calculation on a sticky note instead of recomputing it every time you need it.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting with a table without defining what the state means.
  • Missing a base case or an off-by-one in the table size.
  • Overflow: Fibonacci-like counts grow fast; the problem may ask for the answer modulo 10^9+7.

notes.title: One-dimensional DP
notes.html:
Idea. The state is a single index. dp[i] depends on a few previous values.

Worked example 1: House Robber (max money from non-adjacent houses). dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i]): skip house i or rob it plus the best from two houses back.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int rob(vector<int>& a) {
    int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;                        // best up to i-2 and i-1
    for (int x : a) { int cur = max(prev1, prev2 + x); prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur; }
    return prev1;
}
int rob(int[] a) {
    int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;                        // best up to i-2 and i-1
    for (int x : a) { int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + x); prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur; }
    return prev1;
}
fun rob(a: IntArray): Int {
    var prev2 = 0
    var prev1 = 0                                    // best up to i-2 and i-1
    for (x in a) { val cur = maxOf(prev1, prev2 + x); prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur }
    return prev1
}
def rob(a):
    prev2 = prev1 = 0                                # best up to i-2 and i-1
    for x in a:
        prev2, prev1 = prev1, max(prev1, prev2 + x)
    return prev1

Worked example 2: Coin Change (fewest coins to make amount, or -1). dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int coinChange(vector<int>& coins, int amount) {
    vector<int> dp(amount + 1, amount + 1);          // amount + 1 acts as infinity
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int c : coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);                     // amount + 1 acts as infinity
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int c : coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
fun coinChange(coins: IntArray, amount: Int): Int {
    val dp = IntArray(amount + 1) { amount + 1 }     // amount + 1 acts as infinity
    dp[0] = 0
    for (a in 1..amount)
        for (c in coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = minOf(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return if (dp[amount] > amount) -1 else dp[amount]
}
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = amount + 1                                 # acts as infinity
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return -1 if dp[amount] >= INF else dp[amount]

Complexity. House Robber O(n) time, O(1) space. Coin Change O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space. Greedy fails for coin change with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6.

Industry examples. Payment systems making change, resource allocation, and pricing combinations.

Everyday analogy. Making change at a till: the cheapest way to make 6 is the cheapest way to make a smaller amount plus one coin.

Common interview traps.

  • Initialising the "infinity" with INT_MAX then adding 1 (overflow).
  • Reading a coin larger than the current amount (guard c <= a).
  • Forgetting the -1 for impossible amounts.

notes.title: Two-dimensional DP: grids and strings
notes.html:
Idea. The state has two indices: a cell (r, c) of a grid, or a pair of prefixes (i, j) of two strings.

Worked example 1: Unique Paths (robot moves right or down in an m × n grid). dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1].

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int uniquePaths(int m, int n) {
    vector<int> dp(n, 1);                            // first row: one way to each cell
    for (int r = 1; r < m; r++)
        for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) dp[c] += dp[c - 1];   // up (old dp[c]) + left (dp[c-1])
    return dp[n - 1];
}
int uniquePaths(int m, int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dp, 1);                              // first row: one way to each cell
    for (int r = 1; r < m; r++)
        for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) dp[c] += dp[c - 1];   // up (old dp[c]) + left (dp[c-1])
    return dp[n - 1];
}
fun uniquePaths(m: Int, n: Int): Int {
    val dp = IntArray(n) { 1 }                       // first row: one way to each cell
    for (r in 1 until m)
        for (c in 1 until n) dp[c] += dp[c - 1]      // up (old dp[c]) + left (dp[c-1])
    return dp[n - 1]
}
def unique_paths(m, n):
    dp = [1] * n                                     # first row: one way to each cell
    for _ in range(1, m):
        for c in range(1, n):
            dp[c] += dp[c - 1]                       # up (old dp[c]) + left (dp[c-1])
    return dp[n - 1]

Worked example 2: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS). dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i chars of a and first j chars of b. If the characters match, extend the diagonal; otherwise take the better of dropping one character.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lcs(const string& a, const string& b) {
    int n = a.size(), m = b.size();
    vector<vector<int>> dp(n + 1, vector<int>(m + 1, 0));
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
            dp[i][j] = a[i-1] == b[j-1] ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);
    return dp[n][m];
}
int lcs(String a, String b) {
    int n = a.length(), m = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][m + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
            dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);
    return dp[n][m];
}
fun lcs(a: String, b: String): Int {
    val dp = Array(a.length + 1) { IntArray(b.length + 1) }
    for (i in 1..a.length)
        for (j in 1..b.length)
            dp[i][j] = if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 else maxOf(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[a.length][b.length]
}
def lcs(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[n][m]

Complexity. Unique Paths O(m·n) time, O(n) space after row reduction. LCS O(n·m) time and space (O(min(n, m)) space if you only need the length).

Related. Edit Distance (insert, delete, replace), longest palindromic subsequence, minimum path sum, and many string DP problems follow the same table shape.

Industry examples. diff and Git's merge use LCS-style alignment; spell-check and fuzzy search use edit distance; bioinformatics aligns DNA sequences with the same recurrence.

Everyday analogy. Comparing two shopping lists to find the longest set of items appearing in the same order in both.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up the table size (n + 1) × (m + 1) and the i-1 string indexing.
  • Substring (contiguous) versus subsequence (not necessarily contiguous).
  • In row-reduced versions, iterating in the wrong direction and overwriting values still needed.

notes.title: Knapsack and subset sum
notes.html:
Idea. Choose items under a capacity: each item is either taken or not (0/1 knapsack). State: dp[w] = best value (or reachability) with capacity w. Iterate capacity downward so each item is used at most once.

Worked example: Partition Equal Subset Sum (can the array be split into two subsets with equal sums?). Equivalent to: is there a subset that sums to total / 2?

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canPartition(vector<int>& a) {
    int total = accumulate(a.begin(), a.end(), 0);
    if (total % 2) return false;
    int target = total / 2;
    vector<bool> dp(target + 1, false);
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : a)
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--)            // downward: each item used once
            dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x];
    return dp[target];
}
boolean canPartition(int[] a) {
    int total = Arrays.stream(a).sum();
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
    int target = total / 2;
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : a)
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--)            // downward: each item used once
            dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x];
    return dp[target];
}
fun canPartition(a: IntArray): Boolean {
    val total = a.sum()
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false
    val target = total / 2
    val dp = BooleanArray(target + 1)
    dp[0] = true
    for (x in a)
        for (s in target downTo x)                   // downward: each item used once
            dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x]
    return dp[target]
}
def can_partition(a):
    total = sum(a)
    if total % 2:
        return False
    target = total // 2
    dp = [False] * (target + 1)
    dp[0] = True
    for x in a:
        for s in range(target, x - 1, -1):           # downward: each item used once
            dp[s] = dp[s] or dp[s - x]
    return dp[target]

Complexity. O(n × target) time, O(target) space (pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the value of the sum, not just n).

Unbounded vs 0/1. If items can be reused (coin change), iterate capacity upward; for 0/1 (each item once) iterate downward.

Industry examples. Budget allocation, cargo loading, selecting features within a time budget, and cutting stock problems.

Everyday analogy. Packing a suitcase with a weight limit, choosing each item once.

Common interview traps.

  • Iterating upward for 0/1 problems, which reuses an item.
  • Treating knapsack as polynomial; it is NP-hard in general and only pseudo-polynomial.

notes.title: Longest increasing subsequence
notes.html:
Idea. dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i: 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with a[j] < a[i]. That is O(n²). A faster method keeps tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1; binary search where each element belongs: O(n log n).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lengthOfLIS(vector<int>& a) {
    vector<int> tails;
    for (int x : a) {
        auto it = lower_bound(tails.begin(), tails.end(), x);     // first tail >= x
        if (it == tails.end()) tails.push_back(x);                // extends the longest
        else *it = x;                                             // smaller tail for same length
    }
    return tails.size();
}
int lengthOfLIS(int[] a) {
    int[] tails = new int[a.length];
    int size = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        int i = Arrays.binarySearch(tails, 0, size, x);
        if (i < 0) i = -(i + 1);                                  // first tail >= x
        tails[i] = x;
        if (i == size) size++;                                    // extends the longest
    }
    return size;
}
fun lengthOfLIS(a: IntArray): Int {
    val tails = IntArray(a.size)
    var size = 0
    for (x in a) {
        var i = tails.binarySearch(x, 0, size)
        if (i < 0) i = -(i + 1)                                   // first tail >= x
        tails[i] = x
        if (i == size) size++                                     // extends the longest
    }
    return size
}
from bisect import bisect_left

def length_of_lis(a):
    tails = []
    for x in a:
        i = bisect_left(tails, x)                                 # first tail >= x
        if i == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)                                       # extends the longest
        else:
            tails[i] = x                                          # smaller tail for same length
    return len(tails)

Complexity. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Note tails is not the subsequence itself, only its length is valid; reconstruct the sequence with parent pointers if required.

Industry examples. Patience sorting, version history analysis and scheduling the longest chain of compatible tasks.

Everyday analogy. Stacking cards into piles where each pile's top card is as small as possible, so more cards can still be placed later.

Common interview traps.

  • Using upper_bound for strictly increasing sequences (duplicates).
  • Believing tails is the actual LIS.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Define the state, transition, base case, order and answer, then choose memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up) and reduce memory by keeping only the rows or values you need. 1D DP covers climbing stairs, house robber and coin change; 2D DP covers grid paths and string problems such as LCS and edit distance. 0/1 knapsack iterates capacity downward (each item once), unbounded versions iterate upward. LIS has an O(n²) DP and an O(n log n) binary-search version. Check base cases, off-by-one indexing, infinity overflow and whether greedy is invalid.

questions.promptHtml: How do you recognise a dynamic programming problem and what steps do you follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: DP is the area where unstructured guessing fails most.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The signals are overlapping subproblems (the same smaller question repeats) and optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best answers to smaller pieces), often with words like "count the ways", "minimum cost", "is it possible". I define the state, the transition, the base cases, the evaluation order and where the answer lives, then choose memoization or tabulation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Start from brute-force recursion, notice repeated calls, add a cache (top-down), then optionally convert to a table (bottom-up) and shrink memory to the rows actually needed. Climbing stairs: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], giving O(n) time and O(1) space instead of O(2^n).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int climbStairs(int n) {
    if (n <= 2) return n;
    int a = 1, b = 2;
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}
int climbStairs(int n) {
    if (n <= 2) return n;
    int a = 1, b = 2;
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) { int c = a + b; a = b; b = c; }
    return b;
}
fun climbStairs(n: Int): Int {
    if (n <= 2) return n
    var a = 1
    var b = 2
    for (i in 3..n) { val c = a + b; a = b; b = c }
    return b
}
def climb_stairs(n):
    if n <= 2:
        return n
    a, b = 1, 2
    for _ in range(3, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building a table before defining what a cell means.
  • Missing base cases and off-by-one table sizes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Top-down vs bottom-up? → Top-down is easier to derive and only computes needed states; bottom-up avoids recursion depth and enables space reduction.
  2. Answer modulo 10^9+7? → Take the modulus at every addition.
  3. Why is naive Fibonacci exponential? → Recomputes the same subproblems.

sections.html: Senior moves from recursion to memo to optimised table and explains space reduction.

questions.promptHtml: Find the fewest coins needed to make an amount. Why does greedy fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard DP-versus-greedy question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: dp[a] is the minimum coins for amount a: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c ≤ a, with dp[0] = 0. Greedy fails for coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: greedy picks 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 uses two. O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Use amount + 1 as infinity to avoid overflow when adding 1. Return -1 if dp[amount] is still infinity. Counting the number of ways (instead of the minimum) loops coins in the outer loop to avoid counting permutations.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int coinChange(vector<int>& coins, int amount) {
    vector<int> dp(amount + 1, amount + 1);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int c : coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int c : coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
    return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
}
fun coinChange(coins: IntArray, amount: Int): Int {
    val dp = IntArray(amount + 1) { amount + 1 }
    dp[0] = 0
    for (a in 1..amount)
        for (c in coins)
            if (c <= a) dp[a] = minOf(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return if (dp[amount] > amount) -1 else dp[amount]
}
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = amount + 1
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= a:
                dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return -1 if dp[amount] >= INF else dp[amount]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using INT_MAX as infinity and then adding 1.
  • Forgetting the impossible case.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Count the ways to make the amount? → Coins in the outer loop, amounts in the inner loop.
  2. Each coin used once? → Iterate amounts downward (0/1 knapsack).
  3. Can you do it with BFS? → Yes, as shortest path over amounts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains the loop-order difference between combinations and permutations.

questions.promptHtml: Compute the longest common subsequence of two strings. Define the state and reduce the space.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The model 2D string DP and the basis of diff and edit-distance problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j of b. If a[i-1] == b[j-1] then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, otherwise the maximum of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. O(n·m) time and space; keeping only two rows cuts space to O(min(n, m)).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A subsequence keeps order but may skip characters; a substring must be contiguous (that variant resets to 0 on a mismatch). To reconstruct the sequence, walk back from dp[n][m] following the choices.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lcs(const string& a, const string& b) {
    int n = a.size(), m = b.size();
    vector<vector<int>> dp(n + 1, vector<int>(m + 1, 0));
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
            dp[i][j] = a[i-1] == b[j-1] ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);
    return dp[n][m];
}
int lcs(String a, String b) {
    int n = a.length(), m = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][m + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= m; j++)
            dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);
    return dp[n][m];
}
fun lcs(a: String, b: String): Int {
    val dp = Array(a.length + 1) { IntArray(b.length + 1) }
    for (i in 1..a.length)
        for (j in 1..b.length)
            dp[i][j] = if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 else maxOf(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[a.length][b.length]
}
def lcs(a, b):
    n, m = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            if a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    return dp[n][m]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Confusing subsequence with substring.
  • Off-by-one between table indices and string indices.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Edit distance? → Same table with insert, delete and replace costs.
  2. Print the subsequence? → Backtrack through the table.
  3. Space O(m)? → Two rolling rows.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior relates it to diff, reconstructs the answer and reduces space.

questions.promptHtml: Why do you iterate the capacity downward in 0/1 knapsack but upward for unbounded knapsack?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A subtle detail that separates memorising from understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With a one-dimensional table, iterating capacity downward ensures dp[s - x] still holds the value from before the current item, so the item is used at most once. Iterating upward lets dp[s - x] already include the current item, which allows reuse, the unbounded (coin change) case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Partition Equal Subset Sum reduces to "is a subset sum equal to total/2 reachable?" which is a boolean 0/1 knapsack. Complexity is O(n × target), pseudo-polynomial, because it depends on the numeric value of the target.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canPartition(vector<int>& a) {
    int total = accumulate(a.begin(), a.end(), 0);
    if (total % 2) return false;
    int target = total / 2;
    vector<bool> dp(target + 1, false);
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : a)
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x];
    return dp[target];
}
boolean canPartition(int[] a) {
    int total = Arrays.stream(a).sum();
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
    int target = total / 2;
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
    dp[0] = true;
    for (int x : a)
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x];
    return dp[target];
}
fun canPartition(a: IntArray): Boolean {
    val total = a.sum()
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false
    val target = total / 2
    val dp = BooleanArray(target + 1)
    dp[0] = true
    for (x in a)
        for (s in target downTo x) dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - x]
    return dp[target]
}
def can_partition(a):
    total = sum(a)
    if total % 2:
        return False
    target = total // 2
    dp = [False] * (target + 1)
    dp[0] = True
    for x in a:
        for s in range(target, x - 1, -1):
            dp[s] = dp[s] or dp[s - x]
    return dp[target]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Iterating upward and reusing an item.
  • Calling it polynomial; it is pseudo-polynomial.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Maximise value under a weight limit? → dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val).
  2. Count the subsets? → Add counts instead of OR.
  3. Huge target values? → Meet in the middle or approximation.

questions.promptHtml: Find the length of the longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n).

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests moving from an O(n²) DP to a clever binary-search solution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each number, binary search the first tail that is at least the number; replace it, or append if none. The array length is the LIS length. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
tails stays sorted, so binary search works. Replacing a tail with a smaller value keeps all options open for the future without lengthening the subsequence. The array is not itself the subsequence; reconstruct with parent pointers if needed. Use lower_bound for strictly increasing sequences.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int lengthOfLIS(vector<int>& a) {
    vector<int> tails;
    for (int x : a) {
        auto it = lower_bound(tails.begin(), tails.end(), x);
        if (it == tails.end()) tails.push_back(x);
        else *it = x;
    }
    return tails.size();
}
int lengthOfLIS(int[] a) {
    int[] tails = new int[a.length];
    int size = 0;
    for (int x : a) {
        int i = Arrays.binarySearch(tails, 0, size, x);
        if (i < 0) i = -(i + 1);
        tails[i] = x;
        if (i == size) size++;
    }
    return size;
}
fun lengthOfLIS(a: IntArray): Int {
    val tails = IntArray(a.size)
    var size = 0
    for (x in a) {
        var i = tails.binarySearch(x, 0, size)
        if (i < 0) i = -(i + 1)
        tails[i] = x
        if (i == size) size++
    }
    return size
}
from bisect import bisect_left

def length_of_lis(a):
    tails = []
    for x in a:
        i = bisect_left(tails, x)
        if i == len(tails):
            tails.append(x)
        else:
            tails[i] = x
    return len(tails)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using upper_bound, which allows equal elements (non-strict).
  • Treating tails as the real subsequence.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. O(n²) version? → dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for smaller earlier a[j].
  2. Count the number of LIS? → Track counts alongside lengths in the O(n²) DP.
  3. Russian doll envelopes? → Sort by width ascending and height descending, then LIS on heights.

questions.contextHtml: A product search suggests corrections for misspelled queries by computing the edit distance between the typed query and every product name. With 2 million product names of length ~40 and a 1.6-second budget per request, the O(n·m) DP for each pair takes minutes per request.
questions.promptHtml: How would you make fuzzy matching fast enough?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Runs the same DP on all 2 million names and adds more CPUs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Maximum tolerated distance (1 or 2)? Latency target? Do we need ranking or only candidates? Language and alphabet?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Limit to a maximum distance and add a cheap prefix or length filter before the DP.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Comparing against every name is the bottleneck (2M × 40 × 40 operations = 3.2·10^9 per request).
  4. How I'd verify: Profile candidate counts after each filter.
  5. Root cause: No candidate generation; the expensive DP is applied everywhere.
  6. Fix: Generate a small candidate set first with an n-gram (trigram) inverted index or a BK-tree or a trie with bounded edit distance, then run the exact DP only on those candidates, using the banded DP (only cells within distance k of the diagonal), which is O(k·n) per pair. Stop early when the running minimum exceeds the threshold.
  7. Prevention: Offline index builds, caching popular corrections, quality tests with known misspellings.
  8. Trade-offs: Indexes cost memory and need rebuilding; a distance limit misses heavily misspelled words (fall back to phonetic or embedding-based search).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Names in multiple languages? → Normalise Unicode and use language-specific analysers.
  • Need semantic similarity too? → Add embeddings with approximate nearest neighbour search.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replacing brute-force edit distance with trigram candidate filtering plus a banded DP brought correction latency from seconds to about 15 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: brute force on all names.
  • Hire: candidate generation then exact DP.
  • Strong hire: banded DP, index choice trade-offs and fallbacks.
